title: Spotting odd days
objectives: Use reconstruction error to flag unusual days, and choose a threshold on held-out data.

screens.title: Catch the odd days
screens.prose: A linear autoencoder with 3 codes was trained on 500 ordinary days of 10 stocks. On 150 later days we planted 8 days when each stock moved on its own. The histogram shows each later day's reconstruction error; errors above 8 sit in the last bar.
screens.question: Drag the threshold so that every day above it is a planted odd day, and all 8 are caught.

hints.text: The ordinary days pile up at small errors.
The largest ordinary error is 2.37; the smallest planted one is 5.46.

feedback.correct: Any threshold between 2.37 and 5.46 catches all 8 and nothing else.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Move the threshold into the gap.

byKey.low: Too low: ordinary days with errors above it would be flagged.
byKey.high: Too high: the planted day with the smallest error slips under it.

explain.text: Ordinary days rebuild well, errors up to 2.37. Odd days do not fit the 3 shared drivers, so their errors start at 5.46.

screens.title: An error per day
screens.prose: This is **anomaly detection by reconstruction error**: a model trained on normal days rebuilds normal days well and odd days badly. The table gives three days of three stocks with the model's rebuilds, in per cent.
screens.question: Fill in each day's squared rebuild distance.

hints.text: Subtract, square, add the three squares.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each miss before adding.

byKey.abs2: You added the sizes of the misses. Square each one: $0.81 + 1.21 + 0.81$.

explain.text: Day 2 moves the stocks in opposite directions, so it scores 2.83. Day 3 falls about 3% across the board, a big day, yet rebuilds well: 0.06.

screens.title: Set it on held-out days
screens.prose: The threshold is set on **held-out normal days** the model never trained on, at a high quantile $q$. Ten such days have errors 0.3, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5, 0.55, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9 and 1.4. NumPy's `np.quantile` puts the $q$ quantile at position $(n - 1)q$ of the sorted list, interpolating.
screens.question: What is the 0.9 quantile? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Go 0.1 of the way from 0.9 to 1.4.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find position 8.1 in the sorted list, counting from 0.

byKey.ninth: 0.9 sits at position 8. Position 8.1 is a tenth of the way to 1.4.

explain.text: Position 8.1 lies between 0.9 and 1.4, so the threshold is 0.95. About one normal day in ten will exceed it, if future normal days look like these.

screens.title: Precision and recall
screens.prose: The real model: its threshold is the 0.99 quantile of 100 held-out normal days, 1.62. On the 150 later days it flags 11 days, of which 8 are planted (`stat-learning` l12).
screens.question: What is the precision of these flags? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Precision is the share of flags that are real.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the true flags by all flags.

byKey.recall: 1 is the recall: every planted day was caught. Precision divides by the flags.
byKey.fpr: That is the false-alarm rate among normal days. Precision divides by the flags.

explain.text: 8 of 11 flags are real, precision 0.727, and all 8 planted days are caught. The 3 false alarms are 2.1% of 141 normal days, near the 1% the quantile aimed at.

screens.title: A big day that fits
screens.prose: Day 700 is a market-wide fall: the 10 stocks fell 5.5% on average, the biggest move in the sample. Its reconstruction error is 0.47, below the threshold of 1.62. The bars compare each stock's return with its rebuild.
screens.question: Why does the alarm stay quiet?

options.text: The fall moved every stock along the market driver the code keeps
The model shrinks big days towards the average
options.why: A linear rebuild of a big day in the kept space is just as big. Size alone costs nothing.

options.text: The threshold is too high and should be lowered
options.why: Lowering it to 0.47 would flag many ordinary days. The fall is normal in shape.

options.text: Falls are rare, so the model never saw one before
options.why: It never saw one this size, but the shape, every stock moving with the market, is what it learned.

hints.text: Is the fall unusual in size, or in shape?
Which directions does the 3-code model keep?

feedback.correct: Right. The error measures shape, not size.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the fall breaks the usual pattern across stocks.

explain.text: Reconstruction error flags days whose pattern across stocks is unusual. A large move along the usual drivers rebuilds well, so a big day is not the same as a broken relationship.

screens.title: Set on the days you report
screens.prose: A colleague skips the held-out block and takes the 0.99 quantile of the 150 later days themselves, odd days included. Their threshold is 18.43, and it flags 2 days.
screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The threshold was set on data containing the odd days, so it rose to let most of them through
Nothing: a quantile of the later days is the natural threshold
options.why: The odd days push the 0.99 quantile up to 18.43, so the alarm misses days it should catch.

options.text: Only the quantile: 0.95 would have been right
options.why: Any quantile of contaminated days is pulled up by them. The fix is clean held-out days.

options.text: The model needs retraining on the later days
options.why: The model is fine; the threshold is the problem.

hints.text: What do the later days contain?
The threshold should describe normal days only.

feedback.correct: Right. A threshold must come from clean held-out normal days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the quantile was taken over.

byKey.fine: You treated the later days as clean. Their quantile, 18.43, is set by the odd days themselves.

explain.text: With the odd days inside, the 0.99 quantile lands among them, at 18.43, so only 2 days are flagged. It is also circular: the days being judged set the rule judging them.

screens.title: When everything looks odd
screens.prose: In a second panel, from day 650 four stocks swap sectors for good. With the same model and threshold, days 600 to 649 raise 5 alarms, 4 of them planted days. From day 650, 54% of days raise one.
screens.question: What should the desk do?

options.text: A new regime: retrain, and reset the threshold on recent normal days
Act on every alarm, since each day is genuinely odd
options.why: Each day is odd only against the old pattern. After a lasting change, the alarms carry no news.

options.text: Raise the threshold until the alarms stop coming
options.why: That also hides the genuine odd days. The model, not the threshold, is out of date.

options.text: Ignore it, since the alarm will settle by itself
options.why: The model never adapts on its own. It needs new normal days to learn the new pattern.

hints.text: Is each day odd, or has normal changed?
A model learns normal from its training window.

feedback.correct: Right. A lasting change needs a new model, not more alarms.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a run of alarms is telling you.

explain.text: After the swap the model's idea of normal is wrong, so more than half the days score high. Retrain on recent days once the change is confirmed.

screens.title: The alarm
screens.prose: Score each day by $e(\mathbf{x}) = \lVert \mathbf{x} - g(f(\mathbf{x})) \rVert^2$ with a model trained on normal days. Set $\tau$ as the $q$ quantile of $e$ on held-out normal days, and flag $e(\mathbf{x}) > \tau$. If future normal days are like the held-out ones, about a share $1 - q$ of them raise false alarms.
screens.question: With $q = 0.99$, about how many false alarms do 500 normal days raise?

feedback.generic: Not quite. A share $1 - q$ of normal days exceed $\tau$.

byKey.q: 495 is the number below the threshold.

explain.text: A share $1 - q = 0.01$ of normal days exceed $\tau$, so about 5 in 500, provided they resemble the held-out days.

screens.title: Flag and score
screens.prose: Write the alarm and its scorecard. A day is flagged when its error is strictly above the threshold. Precision is the share of flags that are planted days; recall is the share of planted days flagged. With no flags, report precision 0.0.
screens.question: Write `flag_days`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def flag_days(errors, thr, labels):
    errors = np.asarray(errors, dtype=float)
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    flagged = [int(i) for i in np.where(errors > thr)[0]]
    hits = int(sum(labels[i] == 1 for i in flagged))
    precision = hits / len(flagged) if flagged else 0.0
    planted = int((labels == 1).sum())
    recall = hits / planted if planted else 0.0
    return flagged, precision, recall

screens.title: An alarm for broken relationships
screens.prose: A cross-asset risk desk trains an autoencoder on a year of daily moves in equities, rates, credit and currencies, and alarms when a day's reconstruction error passes the held-out 0.99 quantile. On a day of central bank news, equities fall 4% and bonds rally, as usual.
screens.question: Will the alarm fire, and what is it for?

options.text: Probably not: the moves fit the usual pattern, and the alarm is for broken patterns
Yes, because a 4% fall in equities is an extreme move for one day
options.why: Size alone is not what it measures. A big move in the usual shape rebuilds well.

options.text: It fires on any day with central bank news, whatever the moves
options.why: News that moves assets the usual way leaves the error small.

options.text: Never, because an autoencoder cannot see a market crash at all
options.why: It fires when the pattern breaks, as when stocks and bonds fall together.

hints.text: Does the day break the usual pattern?
Remember the market-wide fall on day 700.

feedback.correct: Right. It flags broken relationships, not big moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the pattern across assets is usual.

explain.text: A stock fall with a bond rally is the usual pattern, so it rebuilds well. The alarm is for days such as stocks and bonds falling together, when hedges stop working.

ideas: A model trained on normal days rebuilds normal days well; a day whose pattern across assets is unusual gets a large reconstruction error.
Set the threshold at a high quantile of held-out normal days; about a share $1 - q$ of future normal days then raise false alarms, if they resemble the held-out ones.
A big move along the usual drivers is not odd, and a lasting regime change calls for retraining, not more alarms.
